content: The report titled To Err is Human highlighted the significant issue of preventable medical errors. It emphasized that between 44,000 and 98,000 individuals die annually in the United States due to such errors. To provide context, in the same year, fewer than 50,000 deaths were attributed to Alzheimer’s disease, and 17,000 deaths were linked to illicit drug use. The report was based on an analysis of multiple studies conducted by various organizations. It called for a coordinated and comprehensive effort involving healthcare providers, government agencies, consumers, and other stakeholders to address this critical issue. The report asserted that the knowledge required to prevent these errors already existed and set an ambitious goal of reducing medical errors by 50% within five years. However, as of 2007, this goal had not yet been achieved, and the exact progress toward this target remained unquantified. In 2001, the Institute of Medicine released another influential report titled Crossing the Quality Chasm, which expanded on many of the points raised in To Err is Human. Both reports have been widely cited in the medical and healthcare communities. The findings and recommendations of To Err is Human inspired the Institute for Healthcare Improvement’s 100,000 Lives Campaign. This campaign, launched to improve patient safety, claimed in 2006 to have prevented an estimated 124,000 deaths over an 18-month period through the implementation of patient safety initiatives in more than 3,000 hospitals.
